diagnosis: The generated future-event descriptions frequently over-predict continuation of the same crisis narrative, assume specific outcomes (e.g., court rulings, negotiation deadlocks), and fail to consider that the next effective-date news may shift to an unrelated topic, lower severity, or a different angle. When historical news contains conflicting signals (escalation and de-escalation), the model tends to predict a moderate continuation rather than anticipating a renewed escalation, an easing, or a completely different story. This leads to large tone errors in risk severity, conflict persistence, and missed topic switches.
suggestions: Explicitly state that the next effective-date news may be about a completely different topic (e.g., unrelated industry development, local news, policy announcement) and if so, the tone should reflect the default severity of that new topic—often neutral or unrelated—rather than forcing a continuation of the historical crisis narrative.

When historical news contains both escalation and de-escalation signals, do not assume a moderate continuation; the next news could be a renewed escalation (e.g., new restrictions, government condemnation) or a completely different angle (e.g., company strategic move). Avoid constructing specific future events like court rulings, meeting outcomes, or diplomatic deals unless their occurrence and predictable direction are strongly implied by the historical news; instead, state the range of possibilities without committing to one scenario.
